facts.text: Africa's plant diversity fell sharply at the start of the Miocene, probably because seasons became more pronounced.
Africa's equatorial forest belt broke apart and rejoined repeatedly through the Miocene.
Through the Miocene the climate slowly cooled towards a series of ice ages.

title: Apes evolve and spread across the Old World

facts.text: Apes first evolved in the early Miocene (Aquitanian and Burdigalian), diversified and became widespread across the Old World.
After Afro-Arabia met Eurasia, hominoids and proboscideans dispersed from Africa into Eurasia.
The earliest claimed upright spine and vertical body plan belongs to Morotopithecus, about 21.6 million years ago.
Later waves reached Eurasia: Griphopithecus in Turkey and Slovakia 15–13.5 million years ago, and Dryopithecus in Europe by 12.5 million years ago.
An 'Out-of-Europe' idea holds that several great ape species evolved in Eurasia during the Miocene.

title: Bengal Fan begins to build

facts.text: Sediment eroded from the rising Himalaya and Tibetan Plateau, carried mostly by the Ganges and Brahmaputra, built the Bengal Fan.
The oldest sediments recovered from the fan so far are of Early Miocene age, so the fan is at least that old.
Their minerals and chemistry show Himalayan origin, so the Himalaya was already a major mountain range 20 million years ago.
It is the largest submarine fan on Earth, about 3,000 km long, 1,430 km wide and up to 16.5 km thick.
Changes in its sediments show Himalayan uplift slowed in the Late Pliocene.

title: Daisy family radiates

facts.text: The geologic time scale lists the daisy family (Compositae) as appearing and diversifying rapidly in the Early Miocene, triggering radiations of rodents, snakes and songbirds.
The family went through a significant adaptive radiation in the Neogene, though its oldest fossil pollen, from Antarctica, is 76-66 million years old.
With over 32,000 species, about 10% of flowering plants, it rivals the orchids as the largest plant family.

title: East Asian summer monsoon takes modern form

facts.text: Global cooling led the East Asian Summer Monsoon to begin taking its modern form in the Early Miocene.
Major phases of Himalayan geology during the Miocene affected Asian monsoon patterns, which were linked to northern glacial periods.
Topographic changes in Africa weakened the Somali Jet while South Asian Summer Monsoon rainfall increased.

title: Tian Shan and Altai mountains rise

facts.text: The geologic time scale lists the Tian Shan and Altai Mountains of Central Asia as forming in the Early Miocene, as part of the Himalayan orogeny.
Both lie in the belt deformed by India's collision with Eurasia; the Siberian Altai is the northernmost region that collision affected.
The Tian Shan rose sharply again in the Late Miocene, blocking westerly winds from the Tarim Basin and drying it.

title: Andes rise fastest in the Miocene

facts.text: Head-on subduction of the new Nazca Plate under South America lifted the Andes, with the greatest effect in the Miocene.
The Altiplano began rising in the Miocene and was a high plateau, second in size only to Tibet, by about 13–11 million years ago.
From the Late Miocene the Altiplano region rose from low elevations to over 3,000 m, and Peru's Western Cordillera, paused since the Oligocene, rose sharply after about 10 Ma.
The Principal Cordillera east of Santiago rose about 20–8 Ma; Colombia's Eastern Ranges exhumed faster 12–3 Ma; the Western Cordillera near Misti rose 9–4 Ma with large ignimbrites.
Atacama Fault movement raised the Chilean Coast Range, an island arc collided with northwestern South America, and Quechua phases (9–8, 7–5 Ma) deformed northern Peru.

title: Cetaceans reach their greatest diversity

facts.text: Whales and dolphins were at their most diverse in the Miocene, with over 20 baleen whale genera against six living today.
Raptorial sperm whales appeared during this baleen whale radiation, apparently evolving to prey on baleen whales.
From around 15 million years ago, modern cetaceans began to reach enormous sizes.

title: Fram Strait opens to the Arctic

facts.text: The Fram Strait opened in the Miocene and became the only route for Atlantic water into the Arctic Ocean until the Quaternary.
Uplift of the continental shelf kept that water from passing through the Barents Seaway.

title: Freshwater diatoms appear

facts.text: Marine diatoms radiated in the Cretaceous, but freshwater diatoms did not appear until the Miocene.
Miocene diatom diversity rose as carbon dioxide and global temperatures fell.
Most modern lineages of diatoms had appeared by the Late Miocene.

title: Grasslands come to dominate as forests dwindle

facts.text: As in the Oligocene, grasses kept spreading through the Miocene and came to dominate much of the world while forests dwindled.
Early Miocene forests gave way to mixed forest-grassland in the Middle Miocene; Oregon was savanna by 12 Ma, and grasslands and savannas were established by about 10 Ma.

Fibrous, fire-tolerant grasses co-evolved with herds of high-crowned grazers, which displaced woodland and browsers; by the Hemingfordian, savanna dominated North America and grazing horses outnumbered browsers.
Ants, termites, grassland mammals and snakes diversified; a cooler, drier climate and spreading open landscapes were a major cause of perissodactyl decline.
Deep grassland soils buried carbon and held water, and grass raised albedo, helping make the climate cooler and drier.

title: Kelp forests appear

facts.text: Kelp forests first appeared in Miocene seas and soon became one of Earth's most productive ecosystems.
With grasslands, kelp forests were one of two new biomes that supported much of Miocene life.
Kelp forests are formed by brown macroalgae and provide a unique habitat for marine organisms.
A wide range of sea life, including fish, uses kelp forests for protection or food.
Especially productive kelp forests tend to occur where oceanographic upwelling delivers cool, nutrient-rich water from depth to the surface layer.

title: Last meridiolestidan mammals

facts.text: Meridiolestidans, mammals that dominated Late Cretaceous South America, last appear in the Miocene of Patagonia.
The last was the mole-like burrowing insectivore Necrolestes, 50 million years after the previous known member.

Meridiolestidans are generally classified within Cladotheria, closer to living marsupials and placental mammals than to monotremes, though one study recovered them as sister to spalacotheriid "symmetrodonts".
A possible meridiolestidan is known from a tooth fragment, now lost, from the Eocene La Meseta Formation of the Antarctic Peninsula.

title: Modern bird groups appear

facts.text: Clearly recognisable dabbling ducks, plovers, typical owls, cockatoos and crows appear in the Miocene.
Crows of the genus Corvus are first recorded about 17 million years ago.
By the end of the epoch, all or nearly all modern bird groups are thought to have been present.

title: Sloth families diversify in the Miocene

facts.text: Sloths diversified in the Miocene, when the major sloth families appeared; diversity waxed and waned, then declined at the epoch's end.
A basal sloth group had already colonized the Antilles by the early Miocene.
Ground sloths evolved early, in the late Paleogene and Neogene, while South America was isolated.
Ground sloths ranged from under 100 kilograms in the Caribbean forms to 3,700–4,100 kilograms in the largest genera Megatherium, Lestodon and Eremotherium.

title: Snakes boom in North America

facts.text: Snakes, once a minor part of North American fauna, rose sharply in number and diversity during the Miocene.
Vipers and elapids first appeared in North America, and colubrids diversified into many modern genera.
The expansion of grasslands in North America led to an explosive radiation among snakes.

title: South American native ungulates lose families

facts.text: Notoungulates lost 45% of their families in the Miocene, though species numbers stayed stable.
By the late Miocene, litopterns and notoungulates were the only surviving South American native ungulate groups.
Notoungulates and other South American native ungulates reached their peak diversity in the Eocene and Oligocene.
The group's diversity declined during the Pliocene and Pleistocene, at the same time as the Great American Interchange let North American ungulates and other mammals enter South America.

title: Ogallala Formation spreads across the Great Plains

facts.text: As the Rockies rose, rivers carried eroded rock east and dumped vast sand and gravel on the gentle plains as overlapping alluvial fans.
These Miocene to early Pliocene deposits form the Ogallala Formation of the central High Plains.
They hold the Ogallala Aquifer, one of the world's largest, under about 450,000 km2 of eight states; it supplies about 30% of US irrigation groundwater.

facts.text: Riversleigh, in Queensland, is Australia's most famous fossil site, with mammals, birds and reptiles of Oligocene and Miocene age.
Its Faunal Zone B dates to the Early Miocene, when the area was very wet rainforest; uncompacted limestone keeps bones three-dimensional.
Later Middle Miocene layers hold a 15-million-year-old platypus relative, Obdurodon, and the oldest modern bandicoots and bilbies.
Large-scale ignimbrite volcanism began in the Central Andes about 23 million years ago and continues today.
North of 21 degrees S, the Oxaya Formation erupted 23 to 18 million years ago.
Calderas of the Altiplano-Puna complex have since produced about 15,000 cubic km of mostly dacitic ignimbrite.
One early eruption, the Verde Ignimbrite from Aguas Calientes caldera 17.2 million years ago, released 140–300 cubic km.
In southern Peru the Chuquibamba (Huaylillas) Ignimbrite came from a VEI 7 super-eruption 14.3 to 13.2 million years ago.
Diatomite layers in a New Zealand crater lake preserved fish, plants, spiders, insects and pollen from a surrounding subtropical forest.

facts.text: A large impact formed the 52 km Karakul crater in Tajikistan, during either the Miocene or the Pliocene.
Its age is estimated at less than 23 million years, or possibly less than 5 million years.

title: Megalodon shark first appears

facts.text: The giant shark megalodon evolved around 23 million years ago.
Megalodon and the sperm whale Livyatan were among the large predators that dominated Neogene oceans.
Its first appearance is disputed: some remains are reported from the Late Oligocene, about 28 million years ago, while other estimates are as young as 16 million years.

contested_note: Megalodon's first appearance is disputed, with estimates from about 28 to 16 million years ago.

facts.text: This Aquitanian deposit in Upper Austria preserves huge numbers of plants, fish, marine mammals and invertebrates from the central Paratethys Sea.

title: Alboran Basin opens and Betic Corridor forms

facts.text: Between 23 and 20 million years ago, spreading thinned the crust south of Spain to 12-15 km, forming the Alboran Basin.
Rotation of Iberia in the early Miocene opened the Betic Corridor, a strait joining the Mediterranean and the Atlantic.
The Valencia Trough opened between the Late Oligocene and early Miocene, at the same time as the Provençal Basin.
Amber from Chiapas, Mexico, holds insects, other arthropods, plant fragments and leaf-surface fungi.

title: Dynamic East Antarctic glaciers in the Early Miocene

facts.text: East Antarctica probably held some glaciers during the early to mid Miocene, 23 to 15 million years ago.
The Ross Sea margin of the East Antarctic Ice Sheet advanced and retreated often during the Early Miocene.
Global temperatures stayed fairly steady through the Oligocene and early Miocene, and Antarctic glaciation waned during that time.
About 15 million years ago the Southern Hemisphere ice cap began to grow to its present form, as oceans cooled partly from the Antarctic Circumpolar Current.

title: Early Miocene granites intrude the High Himalaya

facts.text: Granites of early Miocene age, about 22 million years old, intruded the High Himalayan Crystalline Sequence in many places.
That 30-km-thick metamorphic sequence belongs to the Central Himalayan Domain, the backbone of the orogen with its highest peaks.
The Himalayan orogeny is among the continental collisions that produced leucogranites, pale granites melted from sediment-derived rock in thickened crust.

title: Oligocene Drowning Maximum in New Zealand

facts.text: About 22 million years ago only 18% of present-day New Zealand stood above sea level.
This drowning was very important in the radiation of the moa.
Submerged masses like Zealandia, which includes present-day New Zealand, would be considered a continent.

sources.title: 2.4: Archean Eon - Geosciences LibreTexts (Historical Geology (Bentley et al.))

facts.text: After sinking about 900 m between 25.5 and 21.6 million years ago, the Tibetan Plateau rose by 500 to 1,000 m.
This rise took place between 21.6 and 20.4 million years ago.
The Indo-Australian plate is still driven under the Tibetan Plateau, pushing it up at about 5 mm per year, though erosion reduces the actual gain in height.
The Tibetan Plateau is the world's largest and highest plateau above sea level, with an area of 2,500,000 square kilometres.
Watering-hole deposits in Nebraska hold mass-death assemblages of small rhinos with bear dogs, entelodonts, camels and chalicotheres.
The Pebas Formation of western Amazonia records the Pebas Mega-Wetland, or Lake Pebas, from about 21 to 8 million years ago.
The formation covers about 1,000,000 square km.
Its fauna correlates with those of La Venta in Colombia and Urumaco in Venezuela.
About 20 million years ago some conifer and cycad groups began to diversify as conditions changed.
Gymnosperms, including seed ferns, conifers, cycads and ginkgos, could reproduce by seeds from the Devonian.

sources.title: 10.2: Phanerozoic Diversity of Life (According to the Hard Parts) - Geosciences LibreTexts (Historical Geology (Bentley et al.))

title: East African uplift splits Congo and Nile drainages

facts.text: Around 20 million years ago the western flank of the East African Rift rose, cutting the Great Lakes region off from the Congo basin.
Lake Victoria did not yet exist, and Ethiopian and Ugandan rivers did not yet feed the Egyptian Nile.
The African Great Lakes region holds the source of the Nile and several large lakes of the Nile system, including Lake Victoria, Lake Albert, Lake George and Lake Edward.
The East African Rift is an intracontinental rift basin with active volcanism.

title: First giraffes, hyenas and giant anteaters

facts.text: The first giraffes, hyenas and giant anteaters appear around 20 million years ago.
Bird diversity also increased at this time.

title: First step of Tethys seaway closure

facts.text: In the Early Miocene the Arabian part of Africa collided with Eurasia, cutting the Mediterranean off from the Indian Ocean.
The first step of the seaway's closure, about 20 million years ago, cut water exchange by 90%.
The Atlantic–Indian Ocean link closed as Africa-Arabia moved north and sea level fell while the Antarctic Ice Sheet grew.
By the mid-Burdigalian the collision had built a land bridge joining the two landmasses.

contested_note: Sources date the Tethys closure anywhere from c. 35 Ma to 19-12 Ma; the two-step model (c. 20 and c. 14 Ma) follows the Miocene and Tethys Ocean pages.

facts.text: A land bridge between Afro-Arabia and Eurasia, formed around 20 million years ago, set off the Great Old World Biotic Interchange.
Until then the open Tethyan seaway had kept most animals from crossing between the two landmasses.
Animals crossed both ways; at least 37 Eurasian lineages entered Afro-Arabia during the Burdigalian.
Gomphotheres and deinotheres were the first to leave Africa, reaching India by about 18.3 and Iberia by 18 million years ago.
Perissodactyls reached Africa for the first time when it joined Eurasia.

facts.text: Earth's largest gravity anomaly, a sea-level depression south of India covering about 3 million square km, formed around 20 million years ago.
Models link it to plumes from a sinking Tethys slab spreading low-density material beneath the Indian Ocean.
Uplift of southern Africa about 20 million years ago began a long spell of erosion that removed kilometres of rock.
About 19 million years ago, roughly 70% of all open-ocean shark species disappeared.
Neogene oceans came to be ruled by large predators such as megalodon and Livyatan.
The St Bathans fauna of Central Otago dates from the late Early Miocene, about 19 to 16 million years ago.
It is New Zealand's only Cenozoic land fossil record, with early moa, kiwi and adzebills, tuatara relatives, crocodiles, turtles and many bats.
Later cooling and drying wiped out its subtropical members.
River and lake sediments in California, with rhyolite tuff layers, hold abundant vertebrate bones, teeth and footprints.
Volcanoes built the Vogelsberg in Hesse, Germany, mainly in the Middle Miocene; potassium-argon dates span 18.5-10 million years ago, peaking 17-15 million years ago.
It is Central Europe's largest basalt formation and contiguous volcanic region, about 2,500 km2 of many overlapping volcanoes, not one shield.
Its volcanism was tied to fault-block movement, and it ranks among the largest volcanic centres of the European Cenozoic Rift System.

facts.text: Rifting in Ethiopia began about 18 million years ago at the south end, about 11 near the Afar and perhaps 8–6 in the centre.
The rift formed as the Nubian and Somali plates began to separate along the East African rift system.
Opening of the Gregory rift caused the Afar triple junction to form.

facts.text: The sea flooded the young Gulf of Suez rift in the early Miocene, and the rift then deepened.
Rifting culminated in the Burdigalian, around 18 million years ago.
In the Middle Miocene the Red Sea rift broke apart along its length, with motion shifting to the Dead Sea Transform; seafloor spreading followed.
This site in Shandong, China, has yielded over 600 species, from insects with intact wing veins and colours to birds and mammals.
Iceland, thought to have been built by the Iceland mantle plume, first rose above the ocean about 18-16 million years ago.
The oldest rocks formed above sea level in today's Iceland date to 16.5 million years ago.
The island sits where the Eurasian and North American plates pull apart, above the plume, giving it repeated volcanism and geysers.
Great apes and gibbons are estimated to have split about 18 to 12 million years ago.
Molecular evidence puts the ape ancestral to the modern hominid clade at 18 to 13 million years ago; fossils are too scarce to name it.

facts.text: By the Early Miocene most of the Farallon plate had been consumed and the Pacific-Farallon Ridge neared North America.
Crustal stretching that began about 17 million years ago created the province's landscape of ranges and basins.
Tension thinned and dropped the land west of the Grand Canyon region, forming the province.
Since extension began, parts of the province have moved 60 to 300 km sideways, more in the south than the north.

title: Middle Miocene Climatic Optimum

facts.text: Between roughly 17 and 14 million years ago the climate was about 3 °C warmer than today.
Benthic foraminifera put its onset at 16.9 Ma, peak warmth at 15.3 Ma and its end at 13.8 Ma.
Around 15 million years ago, the warmest part of the Late Cenozoic Ice Age, global temperature averaged about 18.4 °C and the Antarctic ice cap shrank.
A positive carbon isotope shift, the Monterey Carbon Excursion, began just before the optimum and ended just after it.
Columbia River flood basalts, helped by volcanic degassing at plate margins, are seen as the main driver, but cannot explain warming before 16.3 Ma.

contested_note: Whether the Columbia River Basalts drove the Middle Miocene warming is debated: warming began about 16.9 Ma, before their main pulse, and they cannot explain warming before 16.3 Ma.

title: Rapid geomagnetic reversal recorded at Steens Mountain

facts.text: Lava flows at Steens Mountain, Oregon, recorded a field reversal about 16.7 Ma, suggesting the field can shift up to 6 degrees a day.
The reversal ending Chron C5Cr contained a series of reversals and excursions.
In Battle Mountain, Nevada, lava flows show a brief, several-year-long interval during a reversal when the field direction changed by over 50 degrees.
During a reversal the field does not vanish completely, and many poles may form chaotically in different places until it stabilizes again.

title: Columbia River flood basalts erupt

facts.text: In the mid-Miocene, lava flooded the Columbia Plateau and Oregon; this large igneous province emitted 95% of its lava between 16.7 and 15.9 Ma.
The province, linked to the Yellowstone hotspot, totals about 210,000 cubic km; its Roza Member alone held at least 1,500 cubic km.
A mantle plume is the most widely accepted cause, though the question is still debated.
The flood basalts ended the Western Cascades period; Cascade volcanism stayed at a low point from 17 to 9 Ma.
The eruptions are often blamed for the Middle Miocene warming, though that warming began earlier, around 16.9 Ma.

facts.text: The Yellowstone hotspot is thought to have arrived under North America in the Miocene and is still active.
Calderas including McDermitt and Virgin Valley formed 16.5 to 15.5 million years ago as the Steens flood basalts waned.
McDermitt Caldera, made by the hotspot about 16.4 million years ago, formed when a rhyolite lava dome collapsed.
Eruptions such as the Longridge Caldera's, 15.6 million years ago, produced up to 400 cubic km of tuff.
Idaho's Clarkia beds preserve leaves so well that some still show autumn colours when first exposed, before oxidising.
Small amounts of ancient DNA have reportedly been isolated from them.
The beds lie within Columbia River lava flows of the Wanapum Basalts, dated 16.1 to 15.9 million years ago.
The hippopotamus evolved around 16 million years ago.
Unusual conditions in New South Wales preserved microscopic soft-tissue detail, rare in Australia, revealing unknown invertebrate species.

title: Australia begins colliding with Southeast Asia

facts.text: In the Middle Miocene, Australia began to collide with Southeast Asia.
The collision blocked equatorial ocean flow between the western Pacific and Indian Oceans.
By 50 Ma Australia had separated from Antarctica.

Fresh ocean water ventilated its deep basins, ending the long Paratethys anoxia.
The sea then held a tropical to subtropical ecosystem with coral reefs and high biodiversity and endemism.

facts.text: Around 15 million years ago the first mastodons (genus Mammut), bovids and kangaroos appear.
Australian megafauna diversified at the same time.
At least 51 geomagnetic reversals occurred in a 12-million-year period centred on 15 million years ago.
There have been at least 183 reversals over the last 83 million years, on average one about every 450,000 years.
In a period of 3 million years centred on 24 Ma, 13 reversals occurred.
Eras of frequent reversals have been balanced by a few superchrons, long periods with no reversals.

title: Lake Vostok sealed under Antarctic ice

facts.text: Lake Vostok's water is estimated to have been sealed beneath the thick East Antarctic ice about 15 million years ago, when the ice sheet formed.

title: Steinheim impact crater forms

facts.text: The 3.8 km Steinheim crater lies about 40 km southwest of the Ries and is also roughly 15 million years old.
The two were once thought to come from one binary asteroid 14.8 Ma; a 2020 study suggests Steinheim is about 500,000 years younger.

contested_note: Whether Steinheim formed together with the Ries impact is disputed; a 2020 study suggests it is about 500,000 years younger.

conflicts.note: Older binary-asteroid view, same age as the Ries

facts.text: Peru's Pisco Formation is ranked among the most important Lagerstätten, with exceptionally preserved megalodon, penguins, whales, marine crocodiles and aquatic sloths.
An asteroid struck what is now southern Germany 14.808 ± 0.038 million years ago, forming the 24 km Nördlinger Ries crater.
The blast released about 2.4×10^21 joules, the power of 40 million Hiroshima bombs.
Melted surface sand flew up to 450 km and is thought to be the source of moldavite tektites in the Czech Republic.

verification.title: U‐Pb dating of zircons from an impact melt of the Nördlinger Ries crater

facts.text: A wave of extinctions on land and in the sea, the Middle Miocene disruption, followed the warm optimum about 14.8 to 14.5 Ma.
Monitor lizards, chameleons, cordylid lizards, alligators and giant turtles had lived in central Europe during the warm optimum.
The crocodilians Gavialosuchus and Diplocynodon vanished from northern latitudes between 14 and 13.5 Ma.
Cooling wiped out the coral reefs of the Paratethys Sea.
Desmostylians, an order of marine mammals, began a terminal decline after the optimum.

title: Middle Miocene cooling expands East Antarctic ice

facts.text: A major, permanent cooling step between 14.8 and 14.1 Ma, the Middle Miocene Climate Transition, ended the warm optimum.
Cold Antarctic deep water increased and the East Antarctic Ice Sheet expanded, reaching roughly its present size by 14 Ma.
Antarctic summers cooled by at least 8 °C; around 13.94 Ma Transantarctic glaciers turned cold-based as annual temperatures fell 25–30 °C.
A flip in the 41,000-year obliquity cycle around 14.0–13.8 Ma is read as a signal of the ice expansion.
The resulting change in ocean circulation is thought to have caused the Miocene Carbonate Crash in the early Tortonian.

conflicts.note: Miocene § Oceans: marked cooling and Antarctic ice growth from 15 Ma
Southern ice cap starts growing to present form (CITATION NEEDED)

facts.text: The Antarctic Plate began subducting beneath South America about 14 million years ago, forming the Chile Triple Junction.
The Chile Ridge collided with South America near Tierra del Fuego.
The asthenospheric window linked to the triple junction disturbed mantle convection beneath Patagonia, causing an uplift of about 1 km that reversed the Oligocene–Miocene transgression.
As the southern Nazca Plate and Chile Rise were consumed by subduction, the Chile Triple Junction advanced north, and it now lies offshore the Taitao Peninsula at 46°15' S.

conflicts.note: Andean orogeny: Chile Ridge starts subducting at 55 degrees S

facts.text: An Antarctic lake under tundra conditions preserved ostracods down to their soft anatomy.

verification.title: Exceptionally preserved lacustrine ostracods from the Middle Miocene of Antarctica: implications for high-latitude palaeoenvironment at 77° south
verification.venue: Proceedings of the Royal Society B Biological Sciences

title: Sea of Japan opens at both ends

facts.text: By 14 million years ago the Sea of Japan back-arc basin was open to the northeast and southwest, and rising seas further isolated Japan.
The Sea of Japan is a modest ocean basin that opened by back-arc spreading between the volcanic arc of the Japanese islands and the Asian mainland.

sources.title: 6.4: The historical record of plate interactions - Geosciences LibreTexts (Historical Geology (Bentley et al.))

title: Patagonian Desert forms in Andean rain shadow

facts.text: As the southern Andes rose 14 to 12 million years ago, their rain shadow created the Patagonian Desert to the east.
A rain shadow forms when orographic uplift makes weather systems drop their precipitation on one side of a mountain, leaving little moisture for the other side.
Dating of metamorphosed layers suggests the Magallanes Basin and the Andean fold-thrust belt were exhumed between 10 and 4 million years ago.

sources.title: 3.6: Scales of Measurement- Geography - Geosciences LibreTexts (Historical Geology (Bentley et al.))

facts.text: East–west rift valleys in the Lhasa and Himalaya terranes suggest the plateau was close to its modern altitude by about 14 to 8 Ma.
Sudden mafic volcanism and faster uplift 14 to 11 Ma point to delamination of the lithosphere, as seen beneath Tibet.
India kept pushing into Asia through the Neogene, building the Himalayas.
Major phases of Himalayan geology in the Miocene affected Asian monsoon patterns.
Accounts differ: the plateau may have neared its present height by the late Oligocene, yet some suture zones stayed tropical lowlands into the early Miocene.

conflicts.note: Oligocene page: the plateau may have neared its present height by the late Oligocene

title: Final closure of the Tethys seaway

facts.text: The second and final step of the Tethys seaway's closure came around 13.8 Ma, as Antarctic glaciers expanded sharply.
A Mediterranean–Indian Ocean link had briefly reopened in the Langhian before closing for good.
The seaway disappeared as Africa collided with Eurasia in the Turkish–Arabian region.

contested_note: Sources date the Tethys closure anywhere from c. 50 or 35 Ma to 19-12 Ma; the two-step model (c. 20 and c. 14 Ma) follows the Miocene and Tethys Ocean pages.

verification.title: Two-step closure of the Miocene Indian Ocean Gateway to the Mediterranean

title: Badenian Salinity Crisis in the Paratethys

facts.text: Midway through the Middle Miocene, rising central European mountains and falling sea level cut the Paratethys off from the ocean.
Around 13.8 Ma closure of the Bârlad Strait turned the Eastern Paratethys into a saltwater lake.
Starved of fresh water, the Central Paratethys laid down evaporites until about 13.4 Ma, like the later Messinian crisis.
Growing isolation wiped out most small and mid-sized deepwater and open-ocean sharks there.

conflicts.note: Miocene page: evaporite period end date

verification.title: Age of the Badenian salinity crisis; impact of Miocene climate variability on the circum-Mediterranean region

facts.text: La Venta in Colombia is a Lagerstätte with a rich neotropical fauna, including glyptodonts, notoungulates and ground sloths.
The animals lived about 13.8 to 12 million years ago.
The site names the Laventan age, the only South American land-mammal age defined north of the equator.

verification.title: Stratigraphy of a middle Miocene neotropical Lagerstätte (La Venta Site, Colombia)

facts.text: Mount Ōkueyama erupted massively about 13.7 million years ago, possibly VEI 8, larger than any eruption in recorded history.
It was one of several huge eruptions across southwest Japan between 15 and 13 million years ago.
Alkaline lake beds hold articulated fish that died en masse from suffocation during ash falls or rapid acidification.

verification.title: Middle–late Miocene palaeoenvironments, palynological data and a fossil fish Lagerstätte from the Central Kenya Rift (East Africa)

facts.text: After open-marine conditions from 13.36 to 12.65 Ma, the Bârlad Strait reopened and the Central Paratethys turned brackish.
This change caused the Badenian–Sarmatian extinction event.
When the Bârlad Strait reopened, lake levels in the Eastern Paratethys dropped as it became a sea again.
Silicate weathering in China's Qaidam Basin fell sharply around 12.6 Ma, marking a major aridification event.
Sivapithecus, a chimpanzee-sized ape, lived in the Indian subcontinent about 12.5-8.5 million years ago; its fossils come from the Sivalik Hills and Kutch.
Its face resembled an orangutan's, with a concave profile, large cheekbones and close-set eyes, and a Pakistani skull strengthened the link.
One of its species may have been the orangutans' ancestor, probably already separate from the line of chimpanzees, gorillas and humans.

conflicts.note: Sivapithecus body text: oldest dated fossils

verification.title: A partial hominoid innominate from the Miocene of Pakistan: Description and preliminary analyses
verification.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

title: Ashfall Fossil Beds: animals buried by ash

facts.text: Ash from the Bruneau-Jarbidge supereruption, on the Yellowstone hotspot in Idaho, drifted about 1,600 km east and buried animals at a Nebraska waterhole, creating famous mammal bone beds.
Rhino-like Teleoceras, three-toed and one-toed horses, camels and birds lie articulated; one rhino holds an unborn fetus. They died of lung failure from inhaled ash.
The Lagerstätte captures a snapshot of a savanna of grassland and trees under a milder climate than today's.
Bullock Creek in Australia's Northern Territory preserves complete marsupial skulls, the crocodile Baru, an early kangaroo and the horned tortoise Meiolania.

title: Eridanos river builds a North Sea delta

facts.text: By about 12 Ma (a minimum age) the Eridanos, flowing from Lapland across the Baltic region, had reached the North Sea area.
Its sediments built an immense delta, reckoned comparable in size to the modern Amazon's.
Remnants of the Eridanos are found across northern Europe, from the North Sea and the Netherlands in the west to sediments in northern Lapland.
Neogene uplift of the South Swedish Dome deflected the Eridanos from its path across south-central Sweden to a course south of Sweden in the Pliocene.
Around 12 Ma the Paratethys sea became a megalake of over 2.8 million km², reaching from the eastern Alps to Kazakhstan.
Its water was brackish, with salinity mostly 12–14‰.
Tectonically trapped and cut off from the Mediterranean and Indian Ocean, it became an isolated inland sea that gradually disappeared.

conflicts.date_text: at the onset of the late Miocene epoch
conflicts.note: Paratethys lead puts the change at the start of the Late Miocene

title: Pliohippus and the radiation of grazing horses

facts.text: Pliohippus arose from Calippus around 12 Ma; Hipparion, Protohippus and Pliohippus all descend from Merychippus.
Around 10 Ma horses grew larger and developed high-crowned teeth.
Hipparion and its relatives proliferated in North America, and at least one migrated to Asia and Europe.

title: Hotspot supereruptions build the Snake River Plain

facts.text: The western Snake River Plain began forming around 12–11 Ma with eruptions of rhyolite lava and ignimbrite.
The Yellowstone hotspot's Picabo caldera erupted the Arbon Valley Tuff about 10.2 Ma; the Twin Falls field was active 10–8.6 Ma.
Two VEI 8 supereruptions followed: McMullen at 8.99 Ma (at least 1,700 km³) and Grey's Landing at 8.72 Ma (at least 2,800 km³).
From 6.6 Ma the Heise field in eastern Idaho produced four big caldera eruptions, starting with 1,500 km³ of Blacktail Tuff at 6.62 Ma.
Oregon's High Lava Plains propagated west from about 10 Ma while the Snake River Plain advanced east.
Deep-ocean links between the Pacific and the Caribbean through Central America had closed by 12–9.2 Ma; a shallow link lasted until 2.45 Ma at the latest.
The first phase of uplift of the Isthmus of Panama is dated to around 12 Ma.
Islands began forming between the Americas in the Late Miocene, letting ground sloths such as Thinobadistes island-hop north.
Colombia's La Venta fauna is the last purely South American assemblage before the Great American Biotic Interchange.
Zircons in middle Miocene bedrock of northern Colombia suggest a full isthmus, rather than islands, may already have formed by 10 Ma.

conflicts.note: Isthmus of Panama: some experts propose 15 Ma for the first closure

verification.title: How old is the Isthmus of Panama?

facts.text: Between 11.8 and 11.3 Ma the Amazon began flowing as a river across the whole continent.
In the Cretaceous the proto-Amazon had flowed west, as part of a river system draining from Africa.
The Amazon is the largest river in the world by discharge, and the second-longest or longest river system, a title disputed with the Nile.
Its average discharge of about 215,000 to 230,000 cubic meters per second is greater than the next seven largest independent rivers combined.

title: Benguela Upwelling begins

facts.text: The cold, nutrient-rich Benguela Upwelling began in the late Miocene, likely feeding the phytoplankton behind the rich marine fossils of Hondeklip Bay.
Today the cold Benguela Current along the coast helps keep the Namib Desert arid.

title: Decline of Europe's large mammals

facts.text: Europe's large mammal diversity fell significantly during the Late Miocene.
In Iberia, grazers diversified while browsers declined as the climate dried.
Over the Miocene the climate slowly cooled towards a series of ice ages.

title: Giant South American crocodilians die out

facts.text: Giant native crocodilians, including the caiman Purussaurus and the gharial Gryposuchus, died out in the late Miocene, probably as northern South America's wetlands vanished.
Purussaurus was the largest of these Miocene crocodilians.

facts.text: Sebecids, the last sebecosuchians, apparently survived on the Greater Antilles until the late Miocene or early Pliocene.

title: Sparassodonts decline; last borhyaenids

facts.text: South America's sparassodont predators declined from the Late Miocene, possibly due to cooling; borhyaenids are last known from the latest Miocene.

title: Danuvius, a German ape that may have walked upright

facts.text: Danuvius guggenmosi, a great ape from the Hammerschmiede clay pit in southern Germany, is dated magnetostratigraphically to 11.62 million years ago.
Its discoverer argues it both hung in trees and walked upright along branches, an 'extended limb clambering' that may have preceded human bipedalism.
Other researchers say the fragmentary remains differ too little from other fossil apes to show how bipedalism began.

contested_note: Whether Danuvius walked upright, and what it says about the origin of bipedalism, is disputed.

facts.text: Choristoderes, semiaquatic reptiles dating back to the Middle Jurassic, survived the K–Pg extinction but died out in the Miocene, for unclear reasons.
The last was Lazarussuchus, a European genus and the group's only survivor since the early Eocene.
Its last definite remains are Early Miocene, from the Czech Republic; possible remains from southern Germany date to about 11.6 Ma.

conflicts.date_text: 168 to 20 or possibly 11.6 million years ago

facts.text: About 11 Ma the Middle Miocene Warm Interval ended and the much cooler Late Miocene Cool Interval began.
Through the Late Miocene, Earth's climate became increasingly like today's.
Desmostylians, cold-adapted marine mammals, declined during the Middle to Late Miocene cooling, which may have been harsher than earlier cold spells.
The modern Yangtze River is estimated to have originated around 11 Ma.
Sedimentation rates suggest its present outlet is no older than the late Miocene, about 11 Ma.
The Yangtze is the longest river of China and the third-longest in the world.
It rises at Jari Hill in the Tanggula Mountains of the Tibetan Plateau and flows 6,300 kilometers east to the East China Sea.
A major but short-lived warming occurred around 10.8–10.7 Ma, early in the Late Miocene.

verification.title: Middle to late Miocene stepwise climate cooling: Evidence from a high-resolution deep water isotope curve spanning 8 million years

facts.text: Aguas Calientes caldera in the Andes erupted the Tajamar ignimbrite, about 350 km³, between 10.5 and 10.1 Ma.

title: First phase of ancient Lake Idaho

facts.text: Lake Idaho existed in a first phase from about 10.1 to 6.4 Ma, returning from 4.3 to 2.5 Ma.

conflicts.note: Later start suggested by volcanic centers north of Boise

facts.text: Around 10 Ma the first members of the elephant family, Elephantidae, arose in Africa from gomphotheres.
From the Late Miocene many proboscideans evolved ever larger tusks and shortened lower jaws.
Late Miocene climate change drove groups such as amebelodontids and choerolophodontids into decline and extinction.
The first members of modern elephant genera appeared around 6–5 Ma, at the Miocene–Pliocene transition.

title: Greenland's margins uplift, enabling an ice sheet

facts.text: Around 10 Ma Greenland's western margin began to rise, later forming plateaus 2,000–3,000 m high; the eastern uplands followed about 5 Ma.
This uplift made a single coherent Greenland ice sheet possible.
Greenland may have had large glaciers as early as 8–7 Ma, though forests survived there into the Pliocene.

title: Ground sloths island-hop to North America

facts.text: Megalonychid and mylodontid ground sloths had island-hopped to North America by about 10–9 Ma (minimum ages), via islands forming between the Americas before any land bridge.
The earliest North American megalonychid, Pliometanastes, lived in the southern US about 9 Ma.
Some large North American herbivores may have reached South America 10–9 Ma over an incomplete land bridge.
These crossings were an early phase of the Great American Biotic Interchange.

conflicts.note: Timeline of life dates the interchange 9.5 Ma (tagged dubious)

facts.text: Ten-million-year-old hominid apes, Chororapithecus from Ethiopia's Afar rift and Nakalipithecus, are known from East Africa.
The gorilla branch split from the human–chimpanzee branch around 10 Ma.
The Rift Valley in East Africa has been a rich source of hominid fossils for studying human evolution.
The East African Rift is an active continental rift zone.

sources.title: Early expansions of hominins out of Africa

title: Pannonian Sea cut off from Paratethys

facts.text: Uplift of the Carpathians around 10 Ma isolated the Pannonian Sea from the rest of the Paratethys.

title: Rivera plate breaks from the Cocos plate

facts.text: Around 10 Ma the Rivera plate broke away from the Cocos plate off western Mexico and became a microplate.
The Cocos Plate, a remnant of the Farallon Plate, is currently being subducted beneath Central America.
Near Central America the Cocos Plate subducts beneath the North America and Caribbean Plates.

title: Gulf of California begins to open

facts.text: Rifting began opening the Gulf of California 10–6 Ma, tearing the Baja California peninsula northwest from mainland Mexico.
The gulf's opening around 6 Ma let a large river cut its way northeast from it; by 5.5–5 Ma streams had merged into one major river.
Geologists widely interpret the gulf itself as coming into being around 5.3 million years ago, as rifting tore Baja California off the North American plate.
The East Pacific Rise propagated up the middle of the gulf, forming the Gulf of California Rift Zone.

sources.title: Geology of the Bryce Canyon area
Geology of the Grand Canyon area

conflicts.note: Gulf of California page: the gulf came into being c. 5.3 Ma

facts.text: From about 10 Ma calderas of the Altiplano–Puna volcanic complex erupted felsic ignimbrites in four pulses separated by quieter spells.
About 10,000 km³ of ignimbrite erupted between 10 and 1 Ma, over crust 70 km thick.
Mafic magma injected into the lower crust, and an overturn before 10.6 Ma melted crust and started the ignimbrite volcanism.
Volcanism peaked 8–4 Ma with huge eruptions at Cerro Panizos, Coranzulí, Vilama, Cerro Guacha and La Pacana.

conflicts.note: Coranzulí page: APVC activity began 11 Ma

facts.text: Livyatan, a 13.5–17.5 m sperm whale with the largest biting teeth known, hunted off Peru 9.9–8.9 Ma.
Teeth from Chile to Australia suggest it or a close relative ranged widely and survived to about 5 Ma.
Its extinction was probably caused by end-Miocene cooling that reduced its food supply.

title: Last oreodonts; deer and bovids reach North America

facts.text: In North America's Hemphillian age, from about 9.4 Ma, the last oreodonts, mylagaulids and dromomerycids died out.
Deer, bovids, saber-toothed cats and skunks arrived from Asia, while rabbits and short-faced bears diversified.
The Hemphillian North American Land Mammal Age spans 9–4.75 Ma, followed by the Blancan from 4.75–1.6 Ma.
The South Asian winter monsoon strengthened about 9.2–8.5 Ma.
From 7.9 to 5.8 Ma the East Asian winter monsoon grew stronger as the subarctic front shifted south.
Around 5.5 Ma the East Asian winter monsoon intensified rapidly.
At Cerro Ballena in Chile's Atacama Desert, over 40 whales plus seals, sailfish, swordfish, sharks and aquatic sloths were buried in four separate mass deaths.
Toxic algal blooms, fed by high iron levels, likely poisoned them before waves washed the carcasses ashore.
On Gargano, Italy, Miocene mammals and birds fell into fissures in Jurassic rock, building large deposits of well-preserved animals.

title: Lake Malawi basin begins to form

facts.text: The Lake Malawi basin began forming about 8.6 Ma, far earlier than once thought; deep water first appeared 4.5 Ma.
The Malawi rift is part of a linear chain of rift lakes that extends from the southern tip of the Red Sea to Mozambique, with Lake Malawi the southernmost linear lake feature.

sources.title: 12.3: Basins, Sea Level, and Accommodation Space - Geosciences LibreTexts (Historical Geology (Bentley et al.))

facts.text: Vilama caldera in the Andes erupted the enormous Vilama ignimbrite in a VEI 8 eruption about 8.5–8.4 Ma.
The 1,000 km³ Sifon ignimbrite, erupted 8.33 Ma, may also have come from Vilama.

title: Graecopithecus and Ouranopithecus in southeast Europe

facts.text: Graecopithecus and Ouranopithecus, apes from Greece and Anatolia dated to about 8 Ma, have been taken to suggest hominins spread beyond Africa early.
They are probably members of Homininae but not of the human tribe, Hominini.

sources.title: Early expansions of hominins out of Africa

title: Human and chimpanzee lineages split

facts.text: Gibbons, then orangutans, then gorillas branched off before the lines leading to chimpanzees and humans separated; their last common ancestor was probably a small African ape.
A 2026 meta-analysis found that genome-based estimates fitting the fossil record put the split at about 8 Ma, almost certainly more than 7 Ma.
Other molecular estimates range from 10–13 Ma (1998) and 9.3–6.5 Ma (2016) to 6.6–4.7 Ma (2022) and 6.3–5.5 Ma (2025).
Hominin fossils such as Sahelanthropus and Orrorin were at odds with older molecular dates of 6–4 Ma.
The two lineages may have kept exchanging genes as late as 6.3–5.4 Ma.

contested_note: Molecular and fossil-based estimates of the split disagree, ranging from about 13 to 4.7 Ma.

conflicts.note: Miocene lead: split during the Messinian

verification.title: Parting ways: Pan-Homo divergence revisited

title: Leporid Datum: rabbits and hares spread

facts.text: Around 8 Ma rabbits and hares abruptly diversified and spread across the Northern Hemisphere, an event called the Leporid Datum.
By 7 Ma they had expanded into South America and Africa.
Global cooling cut the atmosphere's moisture, driving a worldwide trend towards aridity, especially after 8–7 Ma.
Uplift of East Africa helped shrink its rainforests, and Australia dried as it entered a low-rainfall zone, though its southwest grew wetter 12–8 Ma.
Uplift of the Tian Shan blocked westerly winds and dried the Tarim Basin.
In Kenya's Great Rift Valley aridity rose gradually, with wet episodes still recurring.
One theory links the Sahara's drying to a monsoon weakened when the Tethys Sea dried up around 7 Ma.

title: Banda Arc begins colliding with Australia

facts.text: In the Messinian, the Banda Arc began colliding with Australia and Timor.
It is a standard example of an island arc colliding with a continent to build an orogen.
When an island arc collides with a continent, the subduction zone switches to the other side of the island.

title: Sahelanthropus, earliest known hominin

facts.text: Sahelanthropus, known mainly from the partial skull Toumaï found in northern Chad, lived about 7 Ma; averaged sample ages give 7.2–6.8 Ma.
It is often listed as the first hominin, and the human line of upright-walking apes has been traced back to it.
Some of its anatomy has been proposed, and disputed, as matching the chimpanzee–human last common ancestor.

contested_note: Whether Sahelanthropus is a hominin close to the human–chimpanzee ancestor is disputed.

verification.title: Cosmogenic nuclide dating of Sahelanthropus tchadensis and Australopithecus bahrelghazali : Mio-Pliocene hominids from Chad
verification.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

title: Desmostylians, a marine mammal order, die out

facts.text: Desmostylians, the only known extinct order of marine mammals, died out between 7.2 and 5.3 Ma.
Native to the North Pacific, they declined after the Middle Miocene Climatic Optimum, perhaps because Late Miocene cooling was unusually severe.
The oldest fossils of Thalassocnus, a ground sloth adapted to marine life on South America's Pacific coast, date to roughly 7 Ma in Peru.
It is now known from many Miocene–Pliocene units along South America's coast, including Chile's Coquimbo Formation.
Ground sloths evolved mainly in South America during the late Paleogene and Neogene, while the continent was isolated.
C4 grasses, which use CO2 and water more efficiently than C3 grasses, became ecologically significant between 7 and 6 Ma, though not yet in the north.
As CO2 fell, C4 plants came to dominate grasslands over the last 10 million years.
Silica-rich C4 grasses drove worldwide extinctions of herbivores that lacked high-crowned teeth.
Proposed drivers include falling CO2, or rising seasonality and aridity with monsoon-fed wildfires.
The spread left its imprint on the global carbon cycle, visible in carbon isotope records.

verification.title: Nature's green revolution: the remarkable evolutionary rise of C 4 plants
verification.venue: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B Biological Sciences
verification.note: The abstract says C4 dominance came in the past 10 Myr; 25–32 Myr is the origin of C4 plants.

facts.text: Between 7 and 5.3 Ma temperatures fell sharply, most likely from declining CO2 and a smaller swing in Earth's axial tilt.
Ocean temperatures dropped to near-modern values; extratropical sea surfaces cooled by about 7–9 °C.
Antarctic ice neared its present size, and significant glaciation from 6.26 to 5.50 Ma was paced by 41,000-year obliquity cycles, dominant since 7.7 Ma.
A cold spell around 6 Ma advanced glaciers, lowered sea level and helped start the Messinian salinity crisis.
Around 6 Ma the carbon cycle reorganised: continental carbon stores stopped growing during cold spells.

verification.title: Decreasing Atmospheric CO 2 During the Late Miocene Cooling
1.2 Myr Band of Earth‐Mars Obliquity Modulation on the Evolution of Cold Late Miocene to Warm Early Pliocene Climate
verification.venue: Journal of Geophysical Research Solid Earth

verification.title: CO 2 -forced Late Miocene cooling and ecosystem reorganizations in East Asia
verification.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

facts.text: The oldest mammoth, Mammuthus subplanifrons, appeared in southern and eastern Africa in the Late Miocene, around 6.2-5.3 million years ago.
Mammoths went on to live in Africa, Asia, Europe and North America until about 4,000 years ago.
A 2010 study suggests mammoths and Asian elephants split 7.8-5.8 million years ago, after the African elephant line had branched off 8.8-6.6 million years ago.

conflicts.note: Timeline pages: mammoths first appear 4.8 Ma (the Pliocene event 'Mammoths appear')

facts.text: Fossils of Orrorin tugenensis from Kenya's Lukeino Formation date from 6.1 to 5.7 Ma.
Orrorin appears to have walked upright on two legs about 6 Ma.
Its fossils share no derived features with the great apes.
The rise of bipedal apes at the end of the Miocene sped up faunal turnover in Africa.

title: Trachilos footprints on Crete

facts.text: Possible footprints with hominin-like features on western Crete were dated by cyclostratigraphy to about 6.05 Ma, older than an earlier 5.7 Ma estimate.
If hominin, they would predate other hominin footprints by about two million years; they may instead record an ape that evolved similar feet independently.
Critics doubted they were footprints at all, and the claim clashed with the accepted African origin of hominins.

sources.title: Early expansions of hominins out of Africa

contested_note: Whether the tracks are footprints, and whether a hominin made them, is disputed.

facts.text: Argentavis, a teratorn with a wingspan of 6 m or more and one of the largest flying birds known, soared over South America about 6 Ma.
It may have fed partly on leftovers from Thylacosmilus kills.
As the Mediterranean emptied, the ancestral Nile cut a deep gorge, the Eonile, through Egypt.
Its canyon reached several hundred metres below sea level at Aswan and 2,400 m below at Cairo.
When the sea refilled, the gorge became a gulf that slowly filled with sediment.

title: Messinian salinity crisis: the Mediterranean dries

facts.text: From 5.96 to 5.33 Ma the Mediterranean Sea dried out in cycles of partial or nearly complete desiccation, with evaporites piling up across its floor.
The crisis began basin-wide at 5.96 ± 0.02 Ma, when the Betic corridor and the precursor of the Strait of Gibraltar closed, sealing the sea from the Atlantic.
Causes include plate motion at the Gibraltar Arc, mountain uplift in the western Mediterranean, and glacial sea-level falls of about 10 m from about 6.14 Ma.
After a last closure around 5.6 Ma the basin dried almost completely within a thousand years, and erosion cut canyons on the scale of the Grand Canyon.
Native marine fauna suffered major extinctions; from 5.5 Ma river water diluted the brines into brackish 'Lago Mare' lakes, until the Strait of Gibraltar reopened 5.33 Ma.

facts.text: Cerro Guacha in the Andes erupted the Guacha ignimbrite, roughly 1,200–1,300 km³, about 5.65 Ma.
The genus Ardipithecus appeared around 5.5 Ma, probably after the human–chimpanzee split, while gene flow may still have continued.
An early form, A. kadabba, joined Sahelanthropus and Orrorin among the first hominins in Africa at the very end of the Miocene; Middle Awash fossils date 6.5–5.5 Ma.
The ancestors of humans split from the ancestors of chimpanzees around the end of the Miocene, during the final Messinian Stage (7.5-5.3 Ma).

facts.text: About 5.5 Ma the Caspian Sea, some 30 million years old, became landlocked through tectonic uplift and a fall in sea level.
Pastos Grandes caldera in the Andes erupted the Chuhuilla ignimbrite, about 1,200 km³, 5.45 ± 0.02 Ma, its first caldera-forming cycle.

title: Dead Sea Transform forms as Suez rifting stops

facts.text: Towards the end of the Miocene the Arabian plate began colliding with Eurasia, the Dead Sea Transform developed, and rifting in the Gulf of Suez ceased.
The transform is the boundary between the Arabian and African plates.
The Dead Sea Transform is a left-lateral series of faults between the Sinai Peninsula and the Arabia Plate.
Left steps in this transform have opened a series of wrench basins, including the Dead Sea.

facts.text: About 100 ape species lived across Africa, Asia and Europe during the Miocene.
Europe's apes died out at the end of the Miocene as habitats became more uniform.

title: Khersonian crisis empties the Paratethys megalake

facts.text: Near the end of the Miocene the Khersonian crisis, with rapidly swinging conditions and lake levels, wiped out much of the Paratethys megalake's unique fish fauna.

title: Warming at the end of the Miocene

facts.text: At the end of the Miocene global temperatures rose again as the swing in Earth's axial tilt grew, increasing aridity in Central Asia.
The Pliocene began warmer than the cool Messinian.
The Miocene-Pliocene boundary coincides with the time of the Messinian salinity crisis.
